contentBlocks.text: The Best Windows 95 Games You Can Still Play Today
Posted by Retromash
in Misc
Tagged with

The launch of Windows 95 sparked a new era for PC gaming. It moved away from the DOS command prompt and embraced a more user-friendly, mouse-driven interface. This change laid the groundwork for the modern gaming experiences we enjoy today. There are numerous PC games from that time that not only continue to exist, but have been brought back into existence by officially released remasters, so there is no need for any CD drive or beige tower to play them.

Why Windows 95 Games Still Matter The mid- and late 1990s saw the release of many impressive games. Real-time strategy games found their formula. Action RPGs reached their peak. Point-and-click adventure games reached their creative peak, but soon lost popularity. Commenting on these games isn’t just nostalgia. Many of them laid the foundations for design and are still found in modern releases.

Therefore, they are important for new and returning fans. There’s also an important practical aspect: many of these games have become cheaper and more stable to use than they were on their original hardware platforms. Casino games can also benefit from this development. These games even offer no deposit bonuses, which you can read about at https://www.slotozilla.com/uk/no-deposit-bonus from Slotozilla experts. This is an interesting alternative to action RPGs if you’re looking for something more relaxed.

Windows 95 Games You Can Still Play Today There are five games on this list, which have been selected because of their variety and not because they have the same type or mechanics of game design covered in a different wrapper. A side-by-side comparison will help understand how each of these selections stands up:
The diversity in play styles among these games is striking. They don’t share many traits, showing that they cover a wide range of game genres.

Age of Empires (1997) Microsoft’s ancient world real-time strategy game lets gamers guide a civilization. They started with a few villagers and expanded to a vast empire. This game set the standard for many future RTS games. It is the Definitive Edition of the remastered version of this game that can be downloaded right from Steam, where it has been made by upgrading the graphics of the original and the expansion version Rise of Rome.

Diablo (1996) The Diablo adventure action RPG dropped players inside Tristram Cathedral, into randomly generated levels filled with demons, treasures, and increasingly scarce resources. You can buy it on GOG.com without DRM. There are two options: the original 1996 version or a GOG enhanced version. The enhanced version supports high resolution. This lets you enjoy both the classic and a more user-friendly experience.

RollerCoaster Tycoon (1999) Chris Sawyer’s rollercoaster game allowed users to create increasingly complex rides balancing their budget, guest satisfaction, and of course, an occasional disastrous rollercoaster crash. RollerCoaster Tycoon Deluxe and RollerCoaster Tycoon Classic are on Steam. Deluxe has the original game plus two add-ons: Corkscrew Follies and Loopy Landscapes.

The Curse o f Monkey Island (1997) The third Monkey Island adventure from LucasArts is considered to be one of the most brilliant point and click games of its time, featuring pirate puns and an eccentric cast of characters. The game can be found online on Steam and GOG ; gamers looking for a smoother experience would run it in ScummVM rather than in its default launcher, as save states seem to work better that way.

Quake (1996) Id Software’s sequel to Doom took the first-person shooter genre into full 3D with its industrial gothic style and Trent Reznor music score. Quake Enhanced has been surprisingly active for a project that’s nearly 30 years old. Released in 2021, it’s free for anyone with the game on Steam or GOG. New episodes continued to be made until August 2026, plus a 30th anniversary update was added.

How to Play Windows 95 Games on Modern PCs The vast majority of games listed above overcome their compatibility issues by themselves, because their official remasters are already available natively for the current Windows versions. In case there is no official remaster of some game, several other ways of solving the issue are still possible:
Compatibility mode. Windows still includes built-in compatibility settings that can smooth out issues with older executables, found by right-clicking a game’s shortcut and opening its Properties.
ScummVM. An open-source engine specifically built to run LucasArts-style point-and-click adventures on modern systems, using game files you already legally own.
DOSBox and similar tools. These recreate the environment older DOS and early Windows games expected, and are commonly bundled directly into official GOG releases.
Digital storefront re-releases. As with every game above, publishers frequently handle the technical heavy lifting themselves through Steam, GOG or their own launchers.

Official re-releases are usually better than hunting for old installation disks. Publishers handle licensing and compatibility issues. Plus, they provide a steady flow of new content for Quake. In the cases where no official remastering has been done, looking up the game on a preservation-oriented website like GOG is easier than working out an old version. All of these games require nothing more than a legitimate copy, not even an old beige tower gathering dust in the attic.

Yet there is an odd part to the backlash.... The post As Sony Says, Are CDs Really Going Out of Style? first appeared on Retromash .

As Sony Says, Are CDs Really Going Out of Style?

h1: As Sony Says, Are CDs Really Going Out of Style?
h2: As Sony Says, Are CDs Really Going Out of Style?

contentBlocks.text: As Sony Says, Are CDs Really Going Out of Style?
Posted by Retromash
in Misc
Tagged with

When Sony announced plans to discontinue physical disc production for PlayStation games, the reaction was predictable: some players saw it as another step toward the future, while others saw it as another thing they would lose.

Yet there is an odd part to the backlash. PC gamers have lived with digital game libraries for years through Steam. Digital-first distribution is hardly unusual across gaming and other online services, including platforms such as Jiliplay .
So why does PlayStation’s shift feel different?
It’s All Licenses? Always have been.

The uncomfortable truth is that digital game purchases have always been licenses rather than outright ownership. Steam’s Subscriber Agreement explicitly says its content and services are “licensed, not sold,” with no transfer of ownership to the customer.

PlayStation follows the same broad model. Sony’s software license agreement grants players a limited, non-exclusive, and revocable right to use software on its products rather than transferring ownership of the software itself.
That doesn’t mean buying a digital game is equivalent to renting it for a few days. Players can normally retain access to purchased games under the platform’s terms.
The distinction matters because the platform, rather than the customer, ultimately controls the license, and it becomes all the more noticeable when physical alternatives disappear.
A disc gives players something tangible they can keep, lend, or resell. It can also provide a way to reinstall a game without depending entirely on a digital storefront.
Modern discs aren’t perfect preservation tools, but they give consumers an additional point of control.
Why Steam Gets More Benefit of the Doubt Steam isn’t fundamentally different because its games are digitally licensed. The difference is the environment surrounding that license.

PC gaming is relatively open. Players can modify files, install mods, create unofficial patches, preserve installers, and sometimes build community solutions when an old game stops working. If a publisher abandons a game, the community may have ways to keep it alive.
None of these services are guaranteed. Steam games can still use DRM, disappear from sale, or depend on online services.
Valve’s own agreement also restricts users from modifying, copying, or distributing its content without permission.
But the thing is, PC users simply have more room to work around those restrictions.
There is also a matter of trust. Valve co-founder Gabe Newell and Steam have spent years building a reputation for maintaining a large, convenient digital library.
That reputation doesn’t change the legal nature of a Steam purchase, but it can influence how comfortable people are with the arrangement.
A Steam user might reasonably think, “I don’t technically own the game, but I trust this platform to keep my library accessible.”
That confidence isn’t universal, but it helps explain why the same licensing model can produce a different reaction.
PlayStation Has a Different Problem As for PlayStation, maybe telling your consumer base they don’t own the games they buy with their hard-earned money is not the best idea to build trust.
The bigger issue for PlayStation users is that consoles are closed platforms.

If a PC game develops a compatibility problem, someone can potentially create a fix. If its servers disappear, players might create unofficial alternatives. If the game’s files need modification, the hardware generally allows users to attempt it.
A standard PlayStation doesn’t offer that same freedom.
Players depend much more heavily on the relationship between their account, their console, the PlayStation Store, and the publisher’s infrastructure.
If a game is delisted, becomes dependent on a discontinued service or encounters a problem that the developer no longer supports, ordinary players have fewer ways to intervene.
Physical media becomes more meaningful even for people who prefer buying digitally.

The disc isn’t valuable simply because it is made of plastic. It provides an independent copy of at least part of the game outside the storefront. It can be stored, traded, and retained without requiring the publisher to keep selling it.
Sony itself has acknowledged that physical discs are becoming less central to its business.

In a recent investor Q&A, the company said it plans to discontinue physical disc production and move toward packages containing download codes instead, while arguing that physical media is not a key differentiator between PlayStation and PC.

The Real Question Isn’t Physical vs. Digital Digital distribution is convenient. It eliminates manufacturing and shipping, provides players immediate access, and lets developers update games after release. There are plenty of pragmatic reasons the industry continues moving in that direction.
The concern is what players give up in exchange.
A physical game can be lost or damaged, and modern discs can still depend on downloads and servers. A digital game can be easier to access but is more closely tied to an account and platform.

Knowing that difference becomes especially important for preservation. Ten or twenty years from now, what happens when a storefront changes, a server shuts down or a company decides that an old game is no longer worth supporting?
PC players often have technical options for answering that question themselves. Console players generally have fewer.
That is why the backlash against Sony’s shift isn’t necessarily resistance to digital gaming. Steam already demonstrated that digital libraries can become the norm.
The deeper concern is control .

If a player pays for a game but receives a license rather than ownership, and physical copies eventually disappear, how much control should that player expect to retain over the game after the platform moves on?
That truly is the question underneath the heated argument about whether CDs are going out of style.

articles.title: Flock reportedly tries to shrink workforce with employee buyouts
articles.description: Without buyouts, Flock would "almost certainly" need to lay off staff.

images.caption: Photo of Flock protest signs in Arlington, Virginia.

h1: Flock reportedly tries to shrink workforce with employee buyouts

contentBlocks.text: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now
Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt
Embattled surveillance technology company Flock Safety unveiled a “generous” severance package for voluntary employee departures on Friday, according to a report in Wired .

Flock reportedly expects a significant portion of its 1,500-person workforce to express interest in the buyouts, and said it will grant them to a majority of those who are interested. The company’s internal announcement described these packages as the “most generous” it has ever offered.

By letting employees depart voluntarily, Flock can say goodbye to team members demoralized by the ongoing backlash over the company’s license plate recognition technology. Wired also reports that without buyouts, the company would “almost certainly” need to lay off some staff.

In August, The Washington Post identified 46 cases where police officers have been accused of misusing Flock technology, including cases where they allegedly stalked their wives, girlfriends, or exes. Florida and Texas both said they will stop using the startup’s technology , and an anti-surveillance advocacy group identified 90 cities that dropped Flock in August alone — a fourfold increase from the previous month.
TechCrunch has reached out to Flock for comment. The startup’s CEO Garrett Langley recently told the All-In podcast that the “biggest damage” caused by the backlash has been to “internal morale.”

articles.title: Trump says it’s time to rebrand AI with a new name — and he’s also creating an AI Force
articles.description: Trump claimed, without evidence, that the AI backlash is a Democratic hoax.

images.caption: US President Donald Trump addresses the media on the tarmac after arriving at Paris Orly Airport.

h1: Trump says it’s time to rebrand AI with a new name — and he’s also creating an AI Force

contentBlocks.text: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now
Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt
Trump says it’s time to rebrand AI with a new name — and he’s also creating an AI Force

President Donald Trump has responded in characteristic fashion to the recent debate around AI safety — by declaring that these concerns are part of a long line of hoaxes “generated by the Radical Left Dumocrats, for purposes of destroying our Country.”

On Saturday, Trump began his musings on AI by writing on his social network Truth Social that “many people think that the words ‘Artificial Intelligence’ are inaccurate, and very ineloquent, relative to AI, or Artificial Intelligence.” So he posted a poll where followers could vote on a new name for the technology — Superior Intelligence, Extreme Intelligence, or Supreme Intelligence. (The poll is still ongoing as of publication time.)

A couple hours later, Trump followed up with a post claiming that attempts at “the decimation, or destruction, of AI” are one of “many” Democratic hoaxes, similar to “RUSSIA, RUSSIA, RUSSIA, UKRAINE, UKRAINE, UKRAINE, Global Warming, Impeachment Hoax #1, Impeachment Hoax #2, Men in Women’s Sports, [and] Transgender for Everyone.”

Trump then insisted that he “will not stand by and let this happen,” adding that this so-called hoax “began with an attack on our Data Centers, until people realized how wealthy and prestigious they were for the Communities in which they were built.” But after, in his telling, “the crazed Data Center attack has largely failed,” critics are “going straight at AI.”

Trump did not offer any evidence to back up his claim that widespread suspicion of AI and data centers is not organic and sincere . (Both Republicans and Democrats have taken aim at data centers, and New York recently became the first state to halt permits for large projects .)

The president’s post also echoes his comments at a golf tournament last weekend , when he said he’s open to “guardrails,” but also argued, “I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up.”

On Saturday, Trump went on to say that he will “cherish [the AI industry,] help it, and watch over it, as it grows,” but he’s also forming an AI Force, similar to the Space Force that he established in his first term.
“To that end, I will be announcing, in the near future, the AI ‘Czar’ — Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!” he added.

The president did not say what the AI Force and AI czar’s duties will entail. Venture capitalist David Sacks stepped down as Trump’s AI and crypto czar earlier this year, moving on to co-chair the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.

The AI safety debate recently intensified after an AI researcher said he was quitting Anthropic over concerns that the leading AI companies “earnestly believe it could kill us all by the end of the decade” and are “gambling with our lives.” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently released a plan to “pace the frontier,” which was seemingly endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Critics of the AI industry have suggested that many of these concerns around the technology’s supposed existential threat are a distraction from AI’s more immediate harms .

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, meanwhile, took a call from Trump onstage during the All-In Summit (which Sacks co-hosts), and agreed with the president that the AI backlash is a “hoax,” and insisted that “we’re not going to let” a slowdown happen.

Critics of the AI industry have suggested that many of these concerns around the technology’s supposed existential threat are a distraction from AI’s more immediate harms .

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, meanwhile, took a call from Trump onstage during the All-In Summit (which Sacks co-hosts), and agreed with the president that the AI backlash is a “hoax,” and insisted that “we’re not going to let” a slowdown happen.

articles.title: Google’s Gemini is the latest AI model to hack other companies
articles.description: Google said Gemini had "acted appropriately" by ending each hack immediately.

h1: Google’s Gemini is the latest AI model to hack other companies

contentBlocks.text: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now
Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt
Google’s Gemini accessed the protected systems of three other companies in what The Wall Street Journal reports were the AI model’s first autonomous hacks.

Similar to OpenAI’s breach of Hugging Face , the Gemini hacks were less noteworthy for being particularly sophisticated and more for the fact that they were conducted by an AI model. These breaches took place during cybersecurity testing by a company called Irregular. In one case, Gemini simply guessed passwords until it gained access; in the other two, it found credentials in a public repository.

Irregular reportedly notified Google about the hacks in late July, but the companies did not confirm them publicly until Friday, after the WSJ reached out. Google said it hadn’t previously revealed the hacks because Gemini had “acted appropriately” by ending each breach as soon as it determined it had hacked a real company.

However, Jack Cable, the CEO of AI security company Corridor, told the WSJ that Google was “trying to hide behind the norms that have been created for vulnerability disclosure,” rather than acknowledging that “models are going outside the bounds of what they should be doing, and doing actual cyberattacks.”

articles.title: El día que a Ubisoft se le fue la pinza y convirtió a sus simpáticos conejos en monstruos de pesadilla
articles.description: Si con muchos de los juegos que llegan a nuestras manos ya nos resulta increíble que alguien haya dado luz verde a según qué ideas, imagina lo que podríamos llegar a pensar de todas las que se han quedado por el camino. El Attack of the Killer Rabbids from Outer Space de Ubisoft es el ejemplo perfecto. Aunque las locuras de Ubisoft hace tiempo que dejaron de sorprendernos por lo surrealista de algunas de sus ideas, la de convertir a sus simpáticos Rabbids en una colección de monstruos asesinos a cuál más desagradable es algo que no vimos venir. Ellos tampoco. Los Rabbids asesinos del espacio exterior Estamos en 2010 y en Ubisoft Montpellier vienen de reventar el mercado con unos Rabbids cuyo éxito estaba más que afianzado. Pese a que el protagonismo de los conejos desquiciados tuvo más peso en Wii, los números en PS2 y Xbox 360 no habían funcionado nada mal (14 millones llegaron a colocar entre todas las plataformas). De cara a los próximos meses hay varios proyectos sobre la mesa y, entre cosas más pequeñitas como Michael Jackson: The Experience y el siempre recomendable From Dust , en Montpellier tenían en el horno dos grandes proyectos: Rayman Origins y Attack of the Killer Rabbids from Outer Space . La idea de este último pasa por aprovechar el tirón de los Rabbids pero apuntando a un público más adulto. Con PS3 y Xbox 360 en mente. Lejos de ser simpáticos y alocados animalejos, los conejos serán alienígenas psicópatas sedientos de sangre. Una suerte de venganza idealmente pensada para quienes no soportábamos a las estridentes mascotas. Una en la que disparar a bichos alienígenas con otros tres jugadores consiguiendo muertes y puntos a base de escopetazos y pistolas de rayos al más puro estilo Bulletstorm . ¿Dónde hay que firmar? Aceptamos lagartos por conejos Como cualquier hijo de vecino podría ser capaz de prever, en algún momento del desarrollo alguien debió levantar la mano cuestionándose hasta qué punto era recomendable pervertir la imagen y éxito de uno de sus mayores logros recientes. Y como suele ser lógico en estos casos, decidieron dar un giro a la idea para evitar el desastre. Pensadlo bien, no todos los días se lanza un personaje de la nada y se gana la atención de 14 millones de copias, así que aquello de los Rabbids alienígenas con las tripas colgando y las cuencas de los ojos vacías olía demasiado a suicidio comercial como para no meterle mano. El resultado fue un generoso cambio en el que los conejos dejaron paso a unos escurridizos y viscosos lagartos alienígenas y, bajo el nombre Killer Freaks from Outer Space , la propuesta llegó al E3 de 2011 presentándose como el primer gran exclusivo de Ubisoft para la nueva Nintendo Wii U. Como los cambios del proyecto seguían sin cuajar demasiado, y las características de Wii U terminaron siendo muy diferentes a las de Wii, en cierto punto decidieron desechar el proyecto de los Rabbids y los alienígenas y transformarlo por completo para dar vida a algo más oscuro, adulto y enfocado al juego en solitario. Aprovechando escenarios y armas, pero buscando una forma de llevar más allá el uso de la pantalla del mando de la nueva consola, aquél juego de tiros desenfadado terminó convirtiéndose en algo completamente distinto: el survival horror que a día de hoy todos conocemos por el nombre de ZombiU . articles.title: Brad Bird, Pixar, DreamWorks, Aardman, And More Headline View Conference 2026
articles.description: The five-day event will feature sessions on 'Toy Story 5,' 'Forgotten Island,' 'GOAT,' and more, plus talks on AI and the future of filmmaking.

h1: Brad Bird, Pixar, DreamWorks, Aardman, And More Headline View Conference 2026

contentBlocks.text: Stay informed with free updates
Sign up to get our news digest — delivered directly to your inbox twice a week.

View Conference will return to Turin, Italy, from October 12-16 with a packed five-day program spanning animation, visual effects, games, cinematography, artificial intelligence, and virtual production.

Over the past several years, the English-language event has become an increasingly vital stop for animation and VFX hopefuls heading into awards season, and its 27th edition will feature more than 100 talks, panels, workshops, masterclasses, screenings, and portfolio reviews. Below are some of the biggest attractions headed to Turin for this year’s event.
Brad Bird Looks Ahead To ‘Ray Gunn’
Brad Bird will discuss his long-gestating animated feature Ray Gunn in Welcome to the Future, an hour-long conversation scheduled for October 13.

Bird’s appearance leads a strong group of sessions devoted to major upcoming animated features. Joel Crawford and Januel Mercado, the writer-directors of Dreamworks’ Forgotten Island , will join Pixar’s Kenna Harris ( Toy Story 5 ) and Sony Pictures Animation’s Tyree Dillihay ( GOAT ) for a panel about the future of filmmaking.

Each project will also receive its own spotlight. Harris will lead a behind-the-scenes presentation on Toy Story 5 , while Dillihay will discuss GOAT . Crawford and Mercado will be joined by production designer Ryan Carlson and head of character animation Sean Sexton for a deeper look at Forgotten Island .
Pixar, Disney, Laika, And Aardman Take The Stage

Pixar director Daniel Chong and producer Nicole Paradis Grindle will present a session on the making of Hoppers . Pixar RenderMan artist Dylan Sisson will separately explore RenderMan XPU and the technology’s use on Toy Story 5 .

Disney Animation producer Yvett Merino will talk about the studio’s upcoming holiday release Hexed , while Laika production vfx supervisor Steve Emerson will discuss the studio’s highly anticipated stop-motion fantasy Wildwood .

Aardman director Merlin Crossingham will break down the demands of directing a stop-motion feature, from shaping the larger production to managing its smallest details. Stop-motion artists can also attend a separate four-day puppet lab led by Oscar-winning filmmaker Chris Lavis.
Roger And James Deakins On Cinematography
Two-time Oscar-winning cinematographer Sir Roger Deakins and his longtime creative collaborator James Ellis Deakins will close the conference with Reflections on Cinematography.
The pair will discuss their creative process and careers in a conversation moderated by Cartoon Brew editor-in-chief Jamie Lang.
Several of the year’s largest films will receive dedicated visual-effects presentations.

Wētā FX senior vfx supervisor Eric Saindon will revisit the production of Avatar: Fire and Ash . Oscar winner Andrew Jackson will present a prerecorded session about The Odyssey , while Paul Lambert and Mag Sarnowska will unpack the effects of Project Hail Mary .

ILM animation director Hal Hickel will discuss The Mandalorian and Grogu , including the challenge of animating creatures and characters for live-action environments. Other sessions will cover Spider-Man: Brand New Day , Disclosure Day , Resident Evil , Masters of the Universe , House of the Dragon season three, Coyote vs. Acme , and A24’s Backrooms .

An executive panel featuring ILM head Janet Lewin, Sony Pictures Imageworks president Michelle Grady, and Skydance Animation president Holly Edwards will examine the future of cinema and the businesses creating its imagery.
AI, Games, And The Future Of Production

Artificial intelligence will be a frequent topic of discussion throughout the week, including the panel Every Pixel Will Be Generated, a keynote conversation between NVIDIA media and entertainment vice president Richard Kerris and Runway cofounder and co-CEO Cristobal Valenzuela.
Other panels will examine AI-assisted animation, artist-centered machine-learning tools, automated production, and the technology’s impact on hiring and creative control.

View’s games lineup, an increasingly important part of the event, includes God of War Ragnarök game director Bruno Velazquez, who will explain the game’s one-shot camera approach, along with presentations on Wolverine , Saros , and the Horizon series.

Hands-on programming begins October 12 with workshops covering concept art, Unreal Engine 5, Gaussian splatting, stylized rendering, virtual production, character development, and portfolio preparation. The main conference then moves to Turin’s OGR complex, with select evening screenings held at Cinema Massimo.
The complete schedule and ticket information are available through the VIEW Conference website .

Crawford and Mercado will be joined by production designer Ryan Carlson and head of character animation Sean Sexton for a deeper look at Forgotten Island .

Pixar director Daniel Chong and producer Nicole Paradis Grindle will present a session on the making of Hoppers . Pixar RenderMan artist Dylan Sisson will separately explore RenderMan XPU and the technology’s use on Toy Story 5 .

Disney Animation producer Yvett Merino will talk about the studio’s upcoming holiday release Hexed , while Laika production vfx supervisor Steve Emerson will discuss the studio’s highly anticipated stop-motion fantasy Wildwood .

Aardman director Merlin Crossingham will break down the demands of directing a stop-motion feature, from shaping the larger production to managing its smallest details. Stop-motion artists can also attend a separate four-day puppet lab led by Oscar-winning filmmaker Chris Lavis.

Two-time Oscar-winning cinematographer Sir Roger Deakins and his longtime creative collaborator James Ellis Deakins will close the conference with Reflections on Cinematography.

The pair will discuss their creative process and careers in a conversation moderated by Cartoon Brew editor-in-chief Jamie Lang.

Several of the year’s largest films will receive dedicated visual-effects presentations.

Wētā FX senior vfx supervisor Eric Saindon will revisit the production of Avatar: Fire and Ash . Oscar winner Andrew Jackson will present a prerecorded session about The Odyssey , while Paul Lambert and Mag Sarnowska will unpack the effects of Project Hail Mary .

ILM animation director Hal Hickel will discuss The Mandalorian and Grogu , including the challenge of animating creatures and characters for live-action environments. Other sessions will cover Spider-Man: Brand New Day , Disclosure Day , Resident Evil , Masters of the Universe , House of the Dragon season three, Coyote vs. Acme , and A24’s Backrooms .

An executive panel featuring ILM head Janet Lewin, Sony Pictures Imageworks president Michelle Grady, and Skydance Animation president Holly Edwards will examine the future of cinema and the businesses creating its imagery.

Artificial intelligence will be a frequent topic of discussion throughout the week, including the panel Every Pixel Will Be Generated, a keynote conversation between NVIDIA media and entertainment vice president Richard Kerris and Runway cofounder and co-CEO Cristobal Valenzuela.

Other panels will examine AI-assisted animation, artist-centered machine-learning tools, automated production, and the technology’s impact on hiring and creative control.

View’s games lineup, an increasingly important part of the event, includes God of War Ragnarök game director Bruno Velazquez, who will explain the game’s one-shot camera approach, along with presentations on Wolverine , Saros , and the Horizon series.

Hands-on programming begins October 12 with workshops covering concept art, Unreal Engine 5, Gaussian splatting, stylized rendering, virtual production, character development, and portfolio preparation. The main conference then moves to Turin’s OGR complex, with select evening screenings held at Cinema Massimo.

The complete schedule and ticket information are available through the VIEW Conference website .

articles.title: ‘Coyote Vs. Acme’ Crosses $50 Million Milestone At Domestic Box Office
articles.description: In NA alone, Dave Green's rescued Looney Tunes feature has now grossed more than what Ketchup Entertainment paid for it, with worldwide earnings still growing.

h1: ‘Coyote Vs. Acme’ Crosses $50 Million Milestone At Domestic Box Office

contentBlocks.text: Stay informed with free updates
Sign up to get our news digest — delivered directly to your inbox twice a week.
Coyote vs. Acme has crossed $50 million at the domestic box office, a significant, if symbolic, milestone for a film Warner Bros. once tried to lock away for good.

Ketchup Entertainment’s live-action and animated feature earned $434,090 on Thursday, bringing its domestic total to $50,304,066 after 21 days in theaters, according to Box Office Mojo . It ranked fifth for the day.

Warner Bros. shelved the completed film in 2023, sparking an outcry from filmmakers, artists, and animation fans. Ketchup later acquired its worldwide distribution rights for a reported $50 million. The film’s North American ticket sales alone have now passed that reported price.

That comparison is symbolic, not a break-even calculation. Theaters keep a share of ticket sales, while Ketchup has release and marketing costs. But domestic theaters are only part of the picture. Comscore estimated the film had earned $82.8 million worldwide through last weekend, with several territories still to open. Its worldwide rights also give Ketchup opportunities to earn revenue after the theatrical run, though the terms of any future deals are not public.

And even if the Dave Green-directed film never proves profitable, its release was worth fighting for. A finished film is the culmination of hundreds of artists’ work, and focusing only on profits commoditizes art and culture in an ugly way. Coyote vs Acme ‘s value cannot be limited to numbers on a balance sheet, or by one company’s decision that audiences should never get to see it.

h1: Learning another language may be one of the best ways to keep your brain healthy

contentBlocks.text: Learning another language is a highly complex mental activity . It requires people to remember words, distinguish unfamiliar sounds, recognize patterns, work out grammatical rules, and retrieve the right expression at the right moment. All of this happens while listening, interpreting, and preparing a response.
Could all this mental activity also help keep an aging brain healthier ? Research suggests it can .

Concerns about memory and dementia can send aging adults looking for ways to exercise their brain and maintain cognitive function, whether it is solving crossword puzzles or playing a musical instrument. Language learning might not seem like the same kind of brain exercise, but it is a complex activity that engages several mental processes at once.
I am a linguist who studies language acquisition, use, and loss. My new book, Beyond Words: How We Learn, Use, and Lose Language , examines language and the mind across people’s lifespans.

Research increasingly suggests that language learning and bilingualism can offer cognitive benefits —including for older adults. Learning another language can also create opportunities for communication and social connection.
A person’s brain remains capable of change throughout their life. This ability to adapt in response to experience is known as neuroplasticity.

Learning unfamiliar sounds, vocabulary, and grammatical patterns requires the brain to form and strengthen connections. Language learning engages several mental processes at once, requiring people to absorb and retrieve information , notice when something does not work out, and adjust . This sustained mental effort makes language learning a particularly rich form of cognitive exercise.

Research on bilingualism has found differences in both the brain’s gray matter, which contains neurons and their connections, and white matter, which consists largely of nerve fibers linking different parts of the brain.

Studies have shown greater gray matter density or stronger white matter integrity in bilingual people , compared with people who speak one language. These findings suggest that language experience can be reflected in the brain’s structure, as well as its activity.
But brain differences are only part of the picture.

One reason researchers are interested in language and aging is the idea of cognitive reserve . This term refers to the ability to maintain cognitive function despite age-related changes or damage to the brain.

Bilingualism has been proposed as one factor that can help the brain cope with the effects of aging, because managing two languages places ongoing demands on people’s attention and cognitive control —ultimately helping to strengthen cognitive reserve.

Some studies have found that bilingual people who develop dementia show symptoms at a later age than people who speak one language . This suggests that bilingualism may provide some protection against the effects of brain aging, although it does not necessarily prevent dementia or the brain changes associated with it.
The potential benefit may therefore be greater resilience in the face of those changes, rather than prevention of the underlying disease.
This raises another question: If lifelong bilingualism may help protect the brain as we age, can people gain similar benefits by learning a language later in life?

Age changes the way languages are learned, but adults remain capable of learning new languages throughout life. Adults and kids bring different strengths to the task. Children tend to have advantages with pronunciation and some aspects of grammar, while adults bring larger vocabularies and better-developed strategies for learning.

Research involving older adults suggests that learning a language can produce cognitive benefits, although the findings are mixed . The potential benefit may come less from achieving fluency than from the process of learning itself. Language learning is a sustained challenge that keeps people learning, practicing, and adapting.

There are social benefits, too. Learning another language can deepen cultural understanding , improve interpersonal communication and encourage people to empathize with other people’s perspectives and experiences. It can also connect people with others from different linguistic and cultural backgrounds, creating opportunities for conversation and friendship.

There is no established formula for how much language learning is needed to provide these benefits. Studies have used everything from intensive classroom instruction to short daily sessions with language-learning apps, over periods ranging from weeks to months, to see whether language learning can improve cognitive function. Rather than a magic number of hours, what matters may be sustained engagement in a challenging activity like learning a new language.
Building cognitive resilience
Learning another language is not a miracle cure for aging, and it cannot guarantee protection against Alzheimer’s disease or other forms of dementia.
But it is an unusually rich form of mental activity .

Perhaps the most useful way to think about language learning is not as a way to keep the brain young, but as a way to support cognitive resilience —the ability to keep learning, adapting and functioning despite the changes that come with age.
Aging inevitably changes the brain, but people retain the capacity to learn throughout life. Keeping our brains engaged in demanding new activities may contribute to that resilience.

Karen Stollznow , Senior Research Fellow of Linguistics, University of Colorado Boulder ; Griffith University ; University of New England . This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article .

articles.title: Rings around a tiny body have changed over the past decade
articles.description: Chariklo is only about 250 km across, but it has two rings, and they're changing.

h1: Rings around a tiny body have changed over the past decade

contentBlocks.text: For decades, astronomers thought rings were something only giant planets had. That changed in 2013, when a small, dark body orbiting between Saturn and Uranus passed in front of a star and blinked twice on either side of the main event, revealing two narrow rings around an object barely 250 kilometers across. “It was a surprise,” says Pablo Santos-Sanz, an astronomer at the Instituto de Astrofísica de Andalucía in Granada, Spain. Ever since, the question has been what such rings are made of and how long they can last.

In a recent study, Santos-Sanz and his colleagues used the James Webb Space Telescope to watch the same body, now known as Chariklo, pass in front of a background star again. They found one of its rings had grown denser and the other had almost vanished. We don’t know exactly why.

The technique behind the observation is simple. “We predict when a Solar System object passes in front of a star,” Santos-Sanz said. The starlight dims for a moment, and the shape of that dip reveals the size, shape, and surroundings of the object that caused it. “This is particularly challenging for minor bodies, and more challenging for distant minor bodies,” he said.

The difficulty is that the target’s silhouette on the sky is minuscule, and knowing when it will cross a particular star requires very precise positioning data for both. Still, in 2013, we used ground telescopes to discern Chariklo’s two rings, C1R and C2R. These sat 390 and 405 kilometers from its center and were only a few kilometers wide and about 7 kilometers apart.

Doing this with a space-based telescope, though, makes lining things up considerably harder. JWST sits at the L2 Lagrange point, and controllers need to nudge the telescope every few weeks to keep its orbit stable. “It’s a kind of tricky task,” Santos-Sanz said. His team identified a possible Chariklo occultation in August 2022 and redid the prediction every week. Between the first prediction and one of the last, the projected line of sight shifted by about 110 kilometers, which was enough to move it off the body entirely. Unfortunately, JWST requires observations like this to be planned at least 14 days in advance.

“We did this maybe a bit blindly, because we didn’t know exactly where the line of sight was,” Santos-Sanz said. “I’m going to move one of the biggest, best telescopes in space, and we don’t know if finally we will catch this or not.” But it all worked out.

The occultation came on October 18, 2022. The reconstructed geometry shows JWST’s sightline to the background star skimmed 7.4 kilometers above Chariklo’s surface, missing the body but catching its rings.

JWST recorded the event simultaneously in two near-infrared bands, at 1.5 and 3.2 micrometers, which made it the first time anyone has caught a minor body’s rings in a band beyond three micrometers—a range Earth’s atmosphere puts out of reach for ground telescopes.

The inner ring showed up unmistakably, with abrupt, distinct edges, but it was much darker than before. Averaged over roughly 10 previous ground-based occultations, C1R’s normal opacity (the fraction of starlight it blocks) sat at 0.303. JWST measured it at 0.431. “We didn’t believe it at the beginning, so we fought a lot with the data,” Santos-Sanz said.

The most straightforward explanation was geometry. Rings are not always uniform, and JWST might simply have cut through a denser clump. To rule this scenario out, the team built a lumpy ring model and ran 10 million simulated occultations. Reproducing an opacity as high as JWST recorded came out at a roughly 1 in a 1,000 chance at 1.5 micrometers, and 4 in 100,000 at 3.2 micrometers for a single measurement. The telescope caught the ring twice, going in and coming out, which made the odds even smaller than that.
Santos-Sanz concluded that the inner ring most likely got thicker. At the same time, the outer ring did the opposite.

C2R barely registered at 1.5 micrometers and did not appear at all at 3.2, even though the telescope was recording the same stretch of ring in both bands at the same instant. “At the beginning we didn’t even see the outer ring in the light curve,” Santos-Sanz said. “We had to use models. It was really barely visible, so we said, ‘What is happening here?’”

The team came up with two possible explanations. The first is that JWST, looking at wavelengths where almost no occultation has ever been recorded, is simply seeing grains that scatter light differently in the infrared. The other is that the rings really have physically changed. Santos-Sanz argues radiative transfer models point toward the latter. The older visible-light observations were consistent with a mixture of ice and silicates, but once the JWST data points are added, no combination of materials and grain sizes could explain what the telescope has seen.

“We are witnessing a real evolution of the rings with time,” Santos-Sanz said. “Of course it is not a certainty, but for me it is the preferred explanation.” What’s more, this evolution most likely was not just the material from the fading outer ring migrating inward to the inner ring. Measured as equivalent width, the inner ring gained about 10 times more than the outer ring lost.
“We don’t know where the extra material is coming from, but there are some hypotheses,” Santos-Sanz said.

The leading explanation, Santos-Sanz explains, is a small shepherd satellite sharing the outer ring’s orbit. Such an object should explain the rings’ stability and their sharp edges and could also shed debris that replenishes C1R. “This satellite has not been detected yet, if it exists,” Santos-Sanz said.

A computer model based on JWST data also hints at what the two rings are made of. Santos-Sanz, though, makes it clear that this part of the work is unfinished. “Our feeling after this model is that the inner ring should be composed of bigger particles than the outer ring. The outer ring we think is more dusty,” he said. “But this is a work in progress. I can’t say with certainty, well, this is dusty, this is not.”

The best test, the team argues, would be to catch another Chariklo occultation, this time using visible light, which would separate genuine change from a wavelength effect. “We are searching for new occultations,” Santos-Sanz said. Understanding how rings around small bodies evolve over time, he explains, matters, because Chariklo is not the only one to have them.

Rings are now known around another body from the same category as Chariklo, called Chiron, the dwarf planet Haumea, and the trans-Neptunian object Quaoar. Giant-planet rings are already known to shift over months and years; Saturn’s D ring has measurably shrunk, and Neptune’s Adams arcs rearrange themselves. Now small bodies appear to do it as well.
“I think this work is just a piece of the puzzle,” Santos-Sanz said, “but it could be an important clue for broader studies about the rings around minor bodies and around giant planets.”
Santos-Sanz’s study is published in Science Advances: https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeh4794

articles.title: Si tu DualSense te aburre, la versión más buscada está de rebajas, y en tres colores distintos
articles.description: La serie HyperPop de los mandos DualSense para PS5 es una de las más peculiares en lo que respecta a su llamativa paleta de colores.

h1: Si tu DualSense te aburre, la versión más buscada está de rebajas, y en tres colores distintos

contentBlocks.text: El DualSense de PS5 es uno de los mandos con más versiones de la historia, y mira que ha habido mandos. En esta oferta hablamos, en concreto, del DualSense Rhythm Blue de la serie HyperPop Collection para PlayStation 5, que llega para darle un soplo de aire fresco a tus partidas con un diseño de lo más atrevido.

Cuando pasas bastantes horas frente a la pantalla, sostener un mando cómodo y llamativo cambia por completo la experiencia de juego, y de eso se trata. Esta edición especial destaca por un tono azul vibrante que llama la atención desde el primer momento en que lo sacas de la caja.

Los acabados de esta serie buscan aportar un toque estético muy diferente al modelo blanco tradicional que todos conocemos. Es una opción genial para dar color a la zona de juego o para sumar un segundo mando en casa. Actualmente, el mando DualSense Rhythm Blue de la serie HyperPop Collection vale menos de 73 euros en AliExpress con el código de descuento FSES06, con envío gratis desde España.

Además, también se vende en variantes Remix Green y Techno Red para quienes prefieren otros tonos igual de llamativos. Conseguir esta versión con rebaja en la tienda resulta ideal si querías renovar tu equipo ahorrando dinero. Un mando diferente y muy llamativo En el apartado técnico, la gran estrella sigue siendo la tecnología de retroalimentación háptica que transmite vibraciones detalladas en las manos.

Cada terreno, disparo o fricción en pantalla se percibe con un matiz distinto para aumentar la inmersión. Sentir la tensión del entorno directamente en las palmas hace que la experiencia sea mucho más envolvente. A esto se le suman los conocidos gatillos adaptativos, capaces de ofrecer distintos niveles de resistencia según la acción del juego.

But from what I played at Gamescom, Nodusfall has the potential to shake off those FromSoftware comparisons and come into its own. Read more

images.caption: The concept art for the Qiongqi in Nodusfall.

h1: HoYoverse's Nodusfall might look like Elden Ring, but there's a promising dark fantasy action game here that took me by surprise

contentBlocks.text: Nodusfall, aesthetically at least, is about as far from a typical HoYoverse game as you can get. Gone are the bright colours, cute creatures, and bountiful anime women. In their place, we get all the familiar trappings of dark fantasy: mysterious magics, vicious monsters, and a dingier kind of realism that - and I'm sure we've all thought it - feels a little bit Elden Ring . But from what I played at Gamescom, Nodusfall has the potential to shake off those FromSoftware comparisons and come into its own.

I'll admit to being a little worried at the beginning of my preview after learning it would consist of two boss battles fought in groups of four. After all, the majority of my co-op experience comes from RuneScape , a 25-year-old MMORPG primarily played with a mouse, and nobody wants to let their team down.

But first came the character selection. There were four options available in my demo: two focused around melee combat, two ranged. Both combat styles offered one character with healing-focused abilities which I immediately discounted - too much responsibility. The archer with a mechanical arm though? Inflicting heavy damage from a distance while taking care of any nasty surprises was definitely something I could do. Decision made, it was time to discover how my chosen role would actually play out in battle.

Nodusfall's combat, it turns out, is easy enough to get to grips with. There's your basic attack, which fills a gauge that eventually allows you to unleash a more powerful attack. Next, a secondary move. For my archer, this was a nifty - and enjoyable - bomb arrow which, once embedded in a foe's flesh, dealt extra when hit. Beyond that, each character has four unique abilities that operate based on cooldowns, some more generous than others.

My archer, for example, had an ability that essentially acted as a dodge - enabling her to jump backwards before firing off a powerful arrow - and another where she unleashed a spirit wolf. Since the wolf only deals damage in close quarters, I'd first have to dash towards a foe before using it, then follow it up with the dodge to regain some distance. All this, I should add, depletes stamina, but the bar is a generous one.

And I was thrilled to discover my archer had actual range. I could easily run around the edges of the battlefield, safe in the knowledge my attacks would still land - useful for self-preservation and for helping my fellow teammates out. If a teammate was in need of additional firepower or revival, I could easily weave myself back into the midst of battle. And in this way, it wasn't long before I found myself settling into Nodusfall's surprisingly satisfying fighting rhythm.

As for what you'll be fighting, Nodusfall's enemy design draws inspiration from different mythologies around the world. In the demo, for instance, I fought Qiongqi, a creature from Chinese mythology depicted here as a griffin-like beast, and the Maldrake, your more traditional dragon. And HoYoverse has crafted some truly impressive monster encounters that I found myself wanting to stop and properly appreciate - which is pretty hard when the object of your appreciation is also trying to bite your head off.

Each boss battle is structured the way you'd typically expect - multiple stages, each with a new health bar - but, out of the two, the Maldrake was by far my favourite. Since it's a dragon, it attacks by doing the typical dragon things: fire-breathing, jaw-snapping, wing-whacking. Yet, during the fight's opening stage, I noticed something a little bit odd: human-like arms protruding from its chest. The secret behind these arms reveals itself about midway through the battle, when a knight rips itself out of the Maldrake's torso, killing it in the process. Thus the Maldrake fight becomes the Maldrake Knight fight.

Compared to the fairly slow and predictable dragon, the Maldrake Knight is a dangerously fast sword and polearm wielder who you don't want to get cornered by. It can also unleash puddles of black goo, which sap your health if stepped in. All of the strategies I'd been developing for the dragon had to be immediately thrown aside in order to adapt to this very different enemy who just loved tossing people in the air. And I hope HoYoverse can bring the same fun unpredictability to other fights, creating a similar need for experimentation.

Of course, given Nodusfall is a free-to-play title from a studio best known for its gacha games, there are questions to be asked about how this will be monetised. The developer says characters will be unlockable via continuous play rather than the banner system other HoYoverse games like Genshin Impact employ, and so cosmetic monetisation is being considered. Beyond that, however, specifics are limited so we'll have to wait to learn more.

I didn't know what to expect going into Nodusfall's preview, but I had a surprisingly great time. Combat is fast-paced without ever becoming overwhelming, bosses are compelling, and co-op is engaging while remaining approachable. I am, though, curious to learn more about solo play. As to whether Nodusfall can carve out its own niche among the games it's clearly drawing inspiration from, that remains to be seen. From what I've played, though, it's looking promising and I'll be watching its progress during the coming year.
This preview is based on a preview at Gamescom in Cologne, Germany. HoYoverse provided flights and accommodation.

h1: Yes, The FPGB Mini Handheld Is Being Restocked "In 20 Days", But There's A Catch

contentBlocks.text: You've probably seen a new mini FPGA GAME BOY flying around your feeds recently, and that's for good reason; it's a new, pocketable retro handheld that can play your GB/GBC cartridges made by Funny Playing. We were lucky enough to exclusively reveal the device, alongside being one of the first outlets to have a review sample in our hands.

However, communication from FunnyPlaying is limited not only to ourselves but also to the public. They shadowdropped this out of nowhere, with only 20 units being available worldwide at launch. I even warned FunnyPlaying myself that this is abysmal, and when we publish our news post about it, they'll sell out fast, and that they did, in under 10 minutes after we published our post, in fact.

We asked FunnyPlaying why there were only 20 available, when more would be stocked and how many; their response: "Since there are still some issues, we need to make some improvements. Moreover, we are approaching a National Holiday soon, and there are still 30-50 consoles that can only be sold after the holiday". And it matches their added their "wait for 20 days" text they added to their product listing page .

So, the good news is that a restock is not far away, but the catch is that there's a limited ammount available, which seems like it's going to be a trend with this device: limited batches, randomly dropped, which isn't helpful to anyone really. What we want is stock in the thousands, with a set pre-order time, so that we can all prepare, but this means it will be nabbed up by those that follow FunnyPlaying and cool retro gaming news outlets closely.

I asked FunnyPlaying if they'll be making new colours in the future too, and even if they'd like to collaborate with us on a Retro Dodo edition in transparent colours, to which they responded: "We will continue to sell it and there is a possibility of upgrading it. Yes, hope we can cooperate. And we will also add new colours based on market feedback" , though I doubt a RD edition will ever come to fruition, seeing as their previous marketing efforts are a little on the slow side, but we'll keep pestering.

Our full review will drop next week; I still have some testing to do; it's not perfect. I have noticed my GAME BOY rumble carts don't fit, and the on/off switch can be unreliable, but so far I am having fun with it. Stick around and join our f ree weekly newsletter to keep updated about this handheld and its stock drops in the future.

articles.title: Las nuevas generaciones ya no ven Los Simpson ni pillan las referencias, ¿es por la decadencia de la serie o simplemente ha caducado?
articles.description: Los Simpson está a punto de lanzar su temporada 38: la serie de Matt Groening lleva casi 40 años emitiendo de manera regular nuevos episodios en nuestras pantallas, pero todo ha cambiado.

h1: Las nuevas generaciones ya no ven Los Simpson ni pillan las referencias, ¿es por la decadencia de la serie o simplemente ha caducado?

contentBlocks.text: El otro día, una persona de mi edad a la que apenas conocía me coló una referencia a Los Simpson. Supe que era un guiño porque decía “Ganamos, Lisa” y ahí se incluía el nombre de la protagonista, pero no la logré ubicar en la serie porque nunca he estado tan metida en la cultura de la familia amarilla como para conocerme todos sus memes.

Cuando investigué de dónde venía dicha frase descubrí que pertenecía a la temporada 12, cuando la serie de Matt Groening ya había entrado en una fase de decadencia a la que se abocó a partir de la décima, si bien antes de llegar a un momento crítico que podríamos empezar a marcar a partir de la 16.

El humor de Los Simpson todavía sigue vigente, pero más como un recuerdo de ese momento en el que la serie todavía nos hacía reír y se podía hablar un mismo idioma recuperando los momentos más icónicos que habíamos vivido con ella. Porque ahora eso ya no es posible.

Los Simpson llevan mucho tiempo aquí Después de haber lanzado en Disney Plus episodios especiales como Yellow Mirror durante este verano, Los Simpson está a punto de regresar a la televisión estadounidense a finales de este mes de septiembre con su temporada número 38.

Sí, has leído bien, ya vamos por la 38. Y es que Los Simpson nos lleva acompañando desde hace casi cuatro décadas desde el estreno original de la serie de Matt Groening en 1989, a razón de una temporada por año. Es loable su constancia y el altísimo número de temporadas que tiene a sus espaldas, al tiempo que todavía se siguen lanzando nuevos episodios y la gente los continúa viendo, aunque ya no sea lo mismo que al principio.

Lo sorprendente sería que la acogida de la propuesta se hubiera mantenido inalterable a lo largo del tiempo. Hablamos de casi 40 años. Muchas cosas han cambiado en 40 años. Y el entretenimiento es una de ellas. ¿Por qué ya no vemos Los Simpson? Quizá lo que más nos distancie de Los Simpson en este momento sea el infinito abanico de posibilidades actual.

La familia amarilla nació en un momento en el que la televisión tenía seis canales y ahora ya no es que tengamos decenas de ellos, es que existen las plataformas de streaming con las que seguir multiplicando la cifra de opciones. Hemos dejado de tener la limitación de ver Los Simpson tan solo a mediodía cuando echaban la serie en Antena 3 y nos obligaban a tragarnos las reposiciones constantes de la serie hasta hacernos acabar conociendo todos sus chistes porque no había nada más para ver, a encontrarnos con ella al completo en Disney Plus, pudiendo elegir con libertad cómo disfrutarla.

El problema es que quizá ya no nos interese tanto regresar a esta producción como entonces. Desde su creación, Los Simpson ha servido como inspiración y punto de partida para multitud de series que han sabido elegir lo mejor de su fórmula para reinterpretarlo y ofrecer algo único en el panorama de la animación adulta.

Producciones como Padre de familia o Padre made in USA son un buen ejemplo de cómo el regreso a la familia de clase media estadounidense mediante una suerte de sitcom animada seguía siendo un atractivo reclamo para la audiencia hace unas décadas. Aunque ya Matt Groening quiso diversificar en su fórmula apostando por el humor contemporáneo a través de la ciencia ficción con Futurama o la fantasía medieval con (Des)encanto.

Porque quizá la evasión que necesitemos ahora no pase tan solo por satirizar sobre el presente que estamos viviendo a través de unos personajes que sean un reflejo de la realidad. Para eso ya tenemos las redes sociales, donde no dejamos de ver humor mientras todo se desmorona a nuestro alrededor.

De este modo nos es fácil plantarnos ante una evasión mucha más directa mediante distopías de ciencia ficción antológicas al estilo de Love, Death + Robots de Netflix, que ya poco tiene que ver con Los Simpson, pero sí mucho con el giro que ha tomado el entretenimiento en los últimos años abriéndose hacia muchas direcciones posibles.

O quizá el fallo sea que ya no empatizamos tanto con el ideal sociocultural y los problemas que plantea esa serie y veamos un análisis más interesante sobre lo que nos está pasando mediante producciones como la italiana Cortar por la línea de puntos de Zerocalcare, y sus dos secuelas también para Netflix, que en España nos tocan más cerca por su ambientación europea.

Ahora ya no hablamos como Los Simpson porque Los Simpson ha dejado de hablar nuestro idioma, y tan solo algunas personas que vivieron con fuerza su auge durante ese periodo de mayor repercusión se seguirán comunicando con frases al estilo de “Ganamos, Lisa”.

Aunque ya Matt Groening quiso diversificar en su fórmula apostando por el humor contemporáneo a través de la ciencia ficción con Futurama o la fantasía medieval con (Des)encanto.

Porque quizá la evasión que necesitemos ahora no pase tan solo por satirizar sobre el presente que estamos viviendo a través de unos personajes que sean un reflejo de la realidad. Para eso ya tenemos las redes sociales, donde no dejamos de ver humor mientras todo se desmorona a nuestro alrededor.

De este modo nos es fácil plantarnos ante una evasión mucha más directa mediante distopías de ciencia ficción antológicas al estilo de Love, Death + Robots de Netflix, que ya poco tiene que ver con Los Simpson, pero sí mucho con el giro que ha tomado el entretenimiento en los últimos años abriéndose hacia muchas direcciones posibles.

O quizá el fallo sea que ya no empatizamos tanto con el ideal sociocultural y los problemas que plantea esa serie y veamos un análisis más interesante sobre lo que nos está pasando mediante producciones como la italiana Cortar por la línea de puntos de Zerocalcare, y sus dos secuelas también para Netflix, que en España nos tocan más cerca por su ambientación europea.

Ahora ya no hablamos como Los Simpson porque Los Simpson ha dejado de hablar nuestro idioma, y tan solo algunas personas que vivieron con fuerza su auge durante ese periodo de mayor repercusión se seguirán comunicando con frases al estilo de “Ganamos, Lisa”.

h1: What we've been playing - "the rest of the party is, frankly, absolutely feral, so I've been trying to balance that out"

contentBlocks.text: Hello and welcome back to our regular feature where we write a little about the games we've been playing. This week, it's a Chris Tapsell (that's me!) triple-bill - a triple-Tap? - as the team's been either quite stretched or rightfully enjoying a few days off here and there to catch up from a hectic Gamescom period, leaving me to do a proper bodge job of filling in. Expect the usual mobile game addiction, late review apology, and a rule-bending wildcard (it's not that wild).
Anyway! What have you been playing this week?
Here's another question: do you remember what you were playing last week? You don't have to! The What We've Been Playing archive has you covered.
Pokémon TCG Pocket, iPhone

Let's get the obvious one out of the way first: I play this every day, still. My pack luck has been dreadful with the Team Rocket set - duplicates of shinies I have no interest in (Seaking, anyone?) but still missing genuinely useful cards from the main set such as Team Rocket's Raticate ex. Nightmare. Anyway, I've loved the Rocket set itself - it's offered a rare bit of playfulness, and the artworks have been wonderful on the cards, even if the meta's a little stale.
Star Wars: Zero Company, PC

Yes I know I said the review would be ready soon, and I promise it is actually going to be ready very soon, but: it is not ready right now. I'm still thoroughly enjoying it but finding it slow going, and amid other games that have had deadlines come and go - see: ol' Wolverine - it's had to temporarily go on the back burner. Shout out to the Anakin level though. And hopefully slightly more sophisticated thoughts than this from me are coming actually soon .
Dungeons & Dragons, tabletop

I'm a bit of a newcomer to D&D proper, having dabbled very briefly forever ago but never got going with a regular group. I'm now very much in one, and it's a treat - although progress through the actual "main quest" of our "campaign" is remarkably slow (I gather that's kind of standard).

My character is a Loxodon - think a Kajiit but an elephant-person instead of cat-person - with a background as a kind of wandering cleric. The rest of the party is, frankly, absolutely feral, and so I've been trying to balance that out with a character who wishes to be a bit more of a pacifist. There's also a deeply suspicious Tiefling warlock on our crew, who I've been tasked with keeping an eye on by the DM. It's made me into a kind of cross: part weary Gandalf trying to wrangle stray Hobbits, part chin-stroking Brother William of Baskerville. Most of the time it's a case of my friends trying to hit things they shouldn't, and me subsequently putting them to sleep until they calm down. (And that's very fun).
Moonlighter 2: The Endless Vault, Xbox Series X

Bonus freelancer pick here (or ominous freelance hijacking, if you're feeling naughty). The first Moonlighter game - the one where you sell dusty relics in a shop, then moonlight as a sword-swinging dungeon explorer in search of even more sellable relics - never quite grabbed me as much as I thought it should. This new sequel? I've already sunk way too much time into the moreish roguelike since its early access exit.

The difference here, I think, is that there's always a meaningful new upgrade or shiny weapon or potion enhancement or shop decoration or blobby wobbly pet to save money for. And each one of them can quite drastically change how you approach your next procgen run or shift on the shop floor. It's a really satisfying ride to get stuck on, and the much improved monster bashing doesn't hurt.

articles.title: AI hallucination of Chinese nuclear components almost led to US military attack
articles.description: But the military's overall use of AI seems to be accelerating.

images.caption: Listing image for first story in Most Read: AI hallucination of Chinese nuclear components almost led to US military attack

h1: AI hallucination of Chinese nuclear components almost led to US military attack

contentBlocks.text: The US narrowly avoided boarding a Chinese ship based on an “entirely false” US intelligence report generated with the help of AI tools, according to a CNN report .

That erroneous intelligence, submitted by a US Special Operations Command analyst, suggested the Chinese ship was transporting nuclear arms program components through the Middle East, according to “four sources familiar with the episode” cited by CNN. The US military was preparing to intercept and board the ship, with air support, before officials discovered a chatbot used in generating the report had “inaccurately identified the material the ship was carrying.”
One source told CNN the AI-powered fiasco “almost started a war.”
What’s the worst that can happen?

CNN’s report said the analyst in question used a chatbot to analyze intelligence reports regarding the Chinese ship’s manifest, leading to the near-disastrous result. That chatbot “fused together open-source intelligence with secret signals intelligence in government holdings,” and that information was packaged into an intelligence report that almost set off a disastrous chain of events, according to CNN.

The near-miss is one of the more potent and consequential instances of a hallucinating AI ruining the reliability of a professional report. Since “hallucinating” became the Cambridge Dictionary’s word of the year in 2023 , we’ve seen prominent examples of non-fiction authors , journalists , academic researchers , judges , doctors , police departments , corporate call centers , and more getting taken in by AI tools that simply make something up when their training data doesn’t provide sufficient context . And despite some adorable attempts at “do not hallucinate” prompts , some researchers suggest that it may be impossible to prevent LLMs from hallucinating altogether.

One would hope the US military would be aware of these kinds of problems when relying on AI for analysis of intelligence reports. But the Department of Defense in January rolled out an “AI acceleration strategy” that sought to “make all appropriate data available across federated IT systems for AI exploitation, including mission systems across every service and component.”
“AI is only as good as the data that it receives, and we’re going to make sure that it’s there,” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in rolling out that initiative.

Last December, the Department of Defense announced it would use Google’s Gemini for Government as the basis for its bespoke “GenAI.mil” platform. Last month, the department added Grok for Government as an option on the platform. Anthropic also offers a customized version of Claude for US spy work.

In June, a Pentagon representative bragged to Congress that they use generative AI to help create congressionally mandated reports, and that 1.5 million active DoD personnel have used the military’s generative AI tools.

In 2023 , a State Department “Declaration on Responsible Military Use of Artificial Intelligence and Autonomy” stressed that “principled” use of AI by armed forces “should include careful consideration of risks and benefits, and it should also minimize unintended bias and accidents.” That report also urged that “accountable” use of AI systems must always involve “a human in the loop, a responsible human chain of command and control.”

In the years since then, though, we’ve seen fully autonomous attack drones used in the Russian conflict in Ukraine and tested by NATO-backed military contractors . In March, the Department of Defense blacklisted Anthropic over the company’s opposition to its models’ use in autonomous weapons systems, a move that a federal judge said last month was “unlawful retaliation in violation of the First Amendment.”

The reported near miss comes as extinction-level warnings from AI researchers have led to a newly prominent national conversation on AI safety, including calls for regulation and coordinated research “pacing” from leading frontier AI labs.

articles.title: The Enduring Appeal of Retro Sports Games
articles.description: The unmistakable sound of a joystick clicking and buttons mashing was the soundtrack to many a digital sporting triumph. If you grew up in the 8-bit and 16-bit eras, sports video games weren’t about hyper-realistic graphics or complex physics engines; they were about pure, unadulterated... The post The Enduring Appeal of Retro Sports Games first appeared on Retromash .

images.caption: RetromashThe Enduring Appeal of Retro Sports Games | Retromash
The Enduring Appeal of Retro Sports Games

h1: The Enduring Appeal of Retro Sports Games
h2: The Enduring Appeal of Retro Sports Games

contentBlocks.text: The Enduring Appeal of Retro Sports Games
Posted by Retromash
in Misc
Tagged with

The unmistakable sound of a joystick clicking and buttons mashing was the soundtrack to many a digital sporting triumph. If you grew up in the 8-bit and 16-bit eras, sports video games weren’t about hyper-realistic graphics or complex physics engines; they were about pure, unadulterated fun. From the frantic button-bashing of *Track & Field* to the beautifully simple strategy of *Sensible Soccer*, these games captured the spirit of competition in a way that remains deeply compelling. Decades later, the appeal of these pixelated classics hasn’t faded. It has evolved, becoming a cherished part of our collective gaming history.

These games offered an accessible and often hilarious take on professional sports. They weren’t simulations in the modern sense but rather arcade-style experiences that prioritised playability over realism. This focus on immediate enjoyment is a huge part of why they hold such a special place in our hearts, providing a direct line back to a simpler time in both gaming and our own lives.

Pixelated Pitches and Digital Derbies Early sports games charmed us with their glorious simplicity. Developers had to work within severe technical limitations, which forced them to be creative. This led to a generation of games defined by iconic art styles, memorable soundtracks, and instantly understandable controls. Think of the oversized heads and flaming basketballs in *NBA Jam* or the frantic, side-scrolling action of *Excitebike*. These weren’t just games; they were digital playgrounds where the rules of reality were bent for maximum entertainment.

Games like *Tecmo Bowl* on the NES distilled American football down to a handful of key plays, making it accessible to everyone, not just hardcore fans. You didn’t need an encyclopaedic knowledge of the sport to execute a game-winning touchdown pass. Similarly, football games like *Kick Off 2* and *Sensible Soccer* used a top-down perspective and a one-button control scheme that was easy to learn but incredibly difficult to master. This design philosophy created a perfect balance, offering a low barrier to entry with a high skill ceiling that kept players coming back for more. It’s a design ethos that modern developers often look back on, as expressed in this love letter to the games industry , celebrating the foundations laid by these early titles.

Why We Love Reliving Sporting Glory Retro sports games stay popular for more than just simple mechanics. For many, playing these games is a powerful form of nostalgia. It transports us back to childhood living rooms, sleepovers with friends, and the thrill of mastering a new game. This emotional connection is a key aspect of video game nostalgia and retro gaming, where the experience is as much about reliving personal memories as it is about the game itself. The shared experience of couch co-op, something less common in today’s online-focused world, created lasting bonds and friendly rivalries that we remember fondly.

Beyond personal memories, there’s a growing movement to ensure these digital artefacts aren’t lost to time. Efforts to preserve video game classics are crucial for protecting our cultural heritage. Emulation, fan communities, and the rerelease of classic collections on modern consoles allow new generations to discover what made these games so special. This continued access ensures that the joy of landing a perfect 900 in *Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater* or scoring a last-minute winner in *International Superstar Soccer* can be experienced by everyone.

The Evolution of Athlete Protection Watching the pixelated athletes in games like *California Games* or *720°* take a digital tumble was often a source of amusement. A character might fall off a skateboard, flash for a few seconds, and then get right back up as if nothing happened. There was no concept of concussions or long-term injury, and protective gear was either an aesthetic choice or completely absent. This simplistic approach stands in stark contrast to how athlete safety has evolved in the real world, especially for young people participating in sports.

Over the past few decades, our understanding of sports-related injuries has grown immensely. We now recognise the critical importance of properly designed safety equipment. In sports like BMX and skateboarding, which were staples of the retro gaming scene, the focus on safety has transformed. While a digital character could bounce back from any crash, a real-world participant cannot. This has led to significant advancements in protective gear, from advanced padding to specially engineered lightweight helmets for young riders that offer superior protection without hindering performance. The gear we see today is the result of decades of research into materials science and biomechanics, a world away from the bare-bones approach of the past.

From Arcade Graphics to Real-World Performance While early sports games weren’t realistic, they often succeeded in capturing the *feel* of a sport. The physics in *Track & Field*, which required rhythmic button-mashing to build speed, mimicked the exertion of a real sprint. The way the ball would swerve unpredictably in *Sensible Soccer* after a long shot captured the beautiful chaos of the real game. These mechanics, born from technical constraints, created a unique language of play that players had to learn and master.

Today, the line between video game and reality has blurred significantly. Modern sports simulations like the *FIFA* and *Madden NFL* series boast photorealistic graphics and complex physics engines that model player movements with incredible accuracy. Professional athletes and teams now use these games as training tools to analyse plays and simulate game scenarios. The journey from the simple, abstract representations of the 8-bit era to the sophisticated simulations of today reflects the incredible technological progress of the past 40 years. Yet, for all their complexity, modern games still strive for the same goal as their retro counterparts: to capture the core excitement of the sport.

Keeping the Spirit Alive Safely The legacy of retro sports games is not just about nostalgia; it’s about a timeless design philosophy centred on fun and accessibility. This spirit is kept alive today not only through the preservation of classic titles but also through a new wave of indie games that adopt a retro aesthetic. These “neo-retro” titles combine the simple graphics and intuitive controls of the past with modern design sensibilities, proving that great gameplay never goes out of style.

Communities of old-school gamers keep classics alive through online forums, tournaments, and fan-made updates, ensuring these games continue to be played and celebrated. We can look back on the carefree, no-consequences world of pixelated sports with fondness whilst appreciating how far we’ve come in the real world. We can enjoy the memory of a digital skateboarder dusting themselves off after a cartoonish fall, and at the same time, ensure that today’s young athletes are properly protected when they head out to the park. The spirit of play endures, both on the screen and off it.
